title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A homeowner buys a refrigerator once a decade; a framing contractor buys drywall and studs every Tuesday morning.
epigraph.author: Home Improvement Channel Economics

web_blocks.title: 2.1 Audited Operating Segments & Merchandise Division Revenue Mix

web_blocks.html: Lowe's Companies, Inc. is the world's second-largest home improvement retailer. As of October 30, 2026, it operated 1,762 retail stores and outlets across all 50 U.S. states, totaling 197.0 million square feet of retail space [1, 2]. More than 540 Pro distribution branches and over 120 supply chain sites back those stores [1, 2]. After buying Artisan Design Group (ADG) and Foundation Building Materials (FBM) in FY2025, Lowe's reports two groups [1, 3]. Retail Home Improvement is its primary reportable segment, while 'Other' houses the acquired Pro wholesale and builder-services units [1, 3]. In FY2025 (ended January 30, 2026), consolidated net sales rose 3.1% to $86,286 million [1]. Retail Home Improvement generated $84,078 million, or 97.4% of total sales [1]. The 'Other' segment added $2,208 million (2.6%) during its partial-year ownership window [1]. By Q2 FY2026 (ended July 31, 2026), both ADG and FBM were fully consolidated [3]. Quarterly 'Other' sales scaled to $1,941 million, or 7.5% of consolidated quarterly revenue of $25,956 million—nearly $7.8 billion annualized [3].

Inside Retail Home Improvement, Lowe's groups 14 core product lines into three main divisions plus retail services [1]. Home Décor is the largest at $31,527 million, or 36.5% of FY2025 sales [1]. It covers Appliances, Décor, Flooring, Kitchens & Bath, and Paint [1]. This division anchors Lowe's historic DIY appeal and national appliance lead. Still, big-ticket lines like flooring and custom kitchens track existing-home sales closely [1, 24]. Building Products ranks second at $26,533 million, or 30.7% of FY2025 sales [1]. It spans Building Materials, Electrical, Lumber, Millwork, and Rough Plumbing—the core aisles for small-to-medium contractors [1, 22]. Hardlines generated $24,185 million (28.0% of FY2025 sales) across Hardware, Lawn & Garden, Seasonal & Outdoor Living, and Tools, creating sharp Q2 spring seasonality [1]. Retail 'Other' added $1,833 million (2.2%) from installed sales fees, protection plans, and related services [1]. Sales are overwhelmingly domestic: $86,225 million (99.9%) of FY2025 revenue came from the U.S., with just $61 million from FBM's Canadian branches [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Core Retail Home Improvement still produces nearly all GAAP operating profit (12.16% margin in FY25; 14.77% in Q2 FY26). FBM and ADG add ~$7.8B in annualized sales at near-zero initial GAAP margin due to ~$380M+ in annual intangible amortization and lower wholesale gross margins.

web_blocks.title: 2.2 Segment Profitability Divergence: Retail Cash Cow vs. Wholesale Pro Ramp

web_blocks.html: Note 18 of the FY2025 Form 10-K and Note 13 of the Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q expose a sharp profit gap [1, 3]. Legacy retail stores and newly acquired Pro distribution units run on very different economics [1, 3]. In FY2025, Retail Home Improvement earned $10,223 million in operating income on $84,078 million of sales—a solid 12.16% margin [1]. Inside that segment, employee pay was $11,147 million (13.26% of sales), occupancy costs were $1,932 million (2.30%), and ads were $973 million (1.16%) [1]. By contrast, the 'Other' segment (FBM and ADG) posted a $70 million GAAP operating loss (-3.17% margin) on $2,208 million of partial-year FY2025 sales [1]. Deal costs and purchase-accounting amortization drove that red ink [1]. By Q2 FY2026, 'Other' sales hit $1,941 million, yet GAAP operating income was just $3 million (0.11% margin) [2, 3]. Lowe's books roughly $96 million per quarter (~$384 million annualized) in pre-tax intangible amortization on ADG and FBM customer lists and trademarks, atop thinner wholesale gross margins [2, 3]. This mix effect explains why FY2026 consolidated GAAP operating margin guidance sits at 11.1% (11.5% adjusted): flat-comp retail wage inflation meets lower-margin wholesale scale [2, 22].

web_blocks.title: 2.3 Concrete Real-World Customer Journeys Across Every Channel

web_blocks.html: 1. Home Décor & Appliances (DIY / Do-It-For-Me Homeowner): Picture a suburban homeowner in Charlotte whose 12-year-old French-door fridge breaks on Tuesday night. She visits Lowes.com and asks the OpenAI-powered 'Mylow' assistant to check cabinet clearances and ENERGY STAR rebates [1, 14]. She selects an exclusive Whirlpool or LG unit at $2,200, adding a five-year Lowe's Protection Plan ($250) and haul-away install [1, 14]. Lowe's does not pull that heavy box from a cramped store backroom. Its Market Delivery Model routes the fridge from a regional Bulk Distribution Center through a local cross-dock terminal to a dedicated delivery truck [13]. The unit reaches her kitchen within 48 hours with fewer damage claims [13]. In Q3 FY2026, this model powered Lowe's best quarterly Appliances comp gain in five years and its eighth straight positive quarter [24].

2. Building Products & Hardlines (Small-to-Medium 'Pickup-Truck' Pro): Next, picture an independent kitchen-and-bath remodeler in Dallas running four home jobs at once. At 6:15 a.m., he opens the Lowe's app under his MyLowe's Pro Rewards account, relaunched in early 2025 [1, 14, 23]. He orders 40 sheets of moisture-resistant drywall, copper Rough Plumbing fittings, DeWalt or Kobalt fasteners, and Sherwin-Williams/Valspar paint [1, 14, 23]. He picks two-hour Buy Online, Pick Up in Store (BOPIS) staging under the covered Pro canopy [1, 14, 23]. His annual spend earns tiered rewards, business credit, and a dedicated Pro Sales Manager. He loads his pickup in ten minutes without waiting at retail lanes, and uses Lowe's gig same-day delivery if a job runs short [13, 14]. This small-Pro cohort lifted Lowe's retail Pro mix from roughly 19% in 2019 to about 30% by FY2025 [22, 23].

3. Complex Commercial & Homebuilder Pro (FBM & ADG Branch Network): Finally, picture a commercial framing crew building a 250-unit apartment complex in Phoenix, or a national homebuilder finishing 400 Texas homes. Neither buyer shops retail aisles. Through Foundation Building Materials' 370+ wholesale branches, the framer negotiates project pricing on 18,000 sheets of gypsum wallboard, steel studs, ceilings, and insulation [1, 11, 20]. FBM's boom trucks deliver those loads directly to the fourth floor on a 45-day trade credit line [1, 11, 20]. Meanwhile, the homebuilder hires Artisan Design Group to run design-center flooring, cabinet, and countertop selections across hundreds of buyers, managing warehousing and subcontracted installation [1]. In Q3 FY2026, Lowe's confirmed active pilots letting FBM accounts buy store SKUs on existing FBM credit, plus plans to open roughly 15 new FBM branches in 2026 [20].

web_blocks.title: Brand Architecture: Balancing National Power Brands with High-Margin Private Labels
paragraphs: Lowe's pairs leading national brands with proprietary private labels [1, 22]. Its national lineup includes licensed Craftsman tools, DeWalt, Bosch, Whirlpool, LG, Sherwin-Williams/Valspar, and Toro [1, 22]. Private brands span Kobalt (tools), allen + roth (home décor), Project Source (entry-price essentials), Origin 21 (outdoor living), and ReliaBilt (millwork) [1, 22].

Private labels carry higher gross margins and shield Lowe's from direct online price-matching on identical SKUs [1, 22]. National power brands, in turn, deliver the credibility needed to win brand-loyal Pro tradespeople [1, 22].

book_paragraphs: When you walk into a Lowe's store on a Saturday morning, it is easy to assume you are looking at a simple hardware supermarket. Yet if you and I peel back the FY2025 Form 10-K and Q2 FY2026 Form 10-Q, we discover that Lowe's is really two very different economic machines operating under one corporate roof—and understanding the seam between them is the key to reading its future margins accurately.

The first machine is the legacy Retail Home Improvement franchise: 1,762 cavernous U.S. stores spanning 197 million square feet of indoor selling space, plus open-air garden centers. In FY2025, this retail core generated $84.1 billion of revenue—97.4% of the company—and virtually every dollar of its $10.2 billion in GAAP operating profit. Inside those aisles, sales divide cleanly into three roughly equal pillars. Home Décor is the biggest at $31.5 billion, or 36.5% of consolidated sales, anchored by Appliances, Kitchens & Bath, Flooring, and Paint. This is where Lowe's has historically beaten Home Depot on showroom polish, especially in major appliances, where a homeowner replacing a broken refrigerator or washer wants selection, financing, and reliable next-day delivery. Building Products is the second pillar at $26.5 billion (30.7% of sales)—lumber, rough plumbing, electrical wire, millwork, and concrete—the workhorse aisles where small contractors load their pickup trucks before dawn. Hardlines rounds out the triad at $24.2 billion (28.0% of sales), covering tools, hardware, and seasonal lawn and garden gear that surges every spring when homeowners wake up from winter.

The second machine is brand new, and it lives inside the unassuming 'Other' segment line of Lowe's financial statements. That line holds Artisan Design Group, bought for $1.3 billion in June 2025, and Foundation Building Materials, bought for $8.8 billion in October 2025. Because both deals closed mid-year, they contributed just $2.2 billion in FY2025—a mere 2.6% of sales. By the second quarter of FY2026, however, that wholesale Pro segment had already ramped to $1.94 billion in a single quarter, putting it on an annualized run rate approaching $7.8 billion. Here is the catch you and I must never overlook: in that very same quarter, while Lowe's core retail stores earned a sparkling 14.77% operating margin, the newly acquired FBM and ADG segment reported just $3 million in GAAP operating income—a 0.11% margin.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Wholesale Margins Look Thin at First Glance
book_callouts.text: Do not mistake a 0.11% initial GAAP operating margin in FBM and ADG for a broken business. Wholesale building-materials distribution structurally carries lower gross margins than retail stores, and purchase accounting forces Lowe's to amortize nearly $384 million a year in acquired customer-relationship intangibles. The true test over the next three years is whether procurement savings and cross-selling turn that $10.1 billion bet into genuine economic return on capital.

book_subsections.title: Three Customers, Three Completely Different Buying Habits
paragraphs: To feel how Lowe's actually makes money, follow three real customers through its ecosystem. Start with the suburban homeowner whose refrigerator dies mid-week. She does not want to wrestle a 300-pound stainless-steel box into an SUV. She chats with Lowe's AI assistant Mylow online, buys a Whirlpool unit with a five-year protection plan, and expects white-glove delivery within 48 hours. Lowe's Market Delivery Model fulfills that order from a regional bulk warehouse rather than cluttering store backrooms—a capability that just powered Lowe's strongest Appliances comp in five years during Q3 FY2026.

Next, follow a small residential remodeler who runs a two-truck crew. He buys $80,000 a year in lumber, drywall, and plumbing fixtures. Through MyLowe's Pro Rewards, he orders on his phone at 6 a.m., pulls up to the covered Pro canopy, and rolls out in ten minutes. That 'pickup-truck Pro' segment has been Marvin Ellison's quiet triumph, lifting retail Pro penetration from roughly 19% in 2019 to about 30% today.

Finally, follow the customer Lowe's could never reach before 2025: the commercial framing contractor building a 250-unit apartment complex or the national homebuilder erecting 400 suburban houses. They do not shop retail aisles at all. They demand 45-day trade credit, multi-story boom-truck delivery of thousands of sheets of gypsum wallboard from Foundation Building Materials' 370+ branches, and turnkey flooring and cabinet installation from Artisan Design Group. Connecting Lowe's retail purchasing scale with FBM's commercial branches—and letting FBM contractors swipe their trade credit inside Lowe's stores—is the growth bridge management is actively testing right now.

book_subsections.title: Private Brands, Installed Services, and the Anatomy of a Basket
paragraphs: Once you see how Lowe's serves three distinct customer cohorts, you and I should also examine what actually sits inside those shopping carts—because gross margin in home improvement is won or lost in brand architecture. If Lowe's sold only commoditized national brands whose model numbers could be price-checked in three seconds on a smartphone, gross margins would grind lower every year. Instead, Lowe's deliberately pairs anchor national power brands—Whirlpool, LG, DeWalt, Bosch, Sherwin-Williams, and licensed Craftsman tools—with high-margin proprietary private labels like Kobalt in tools, allen + roth in lighting and home décor, Project Source in opening-price-point essentials, Origin 21 in patio furniture, and ReliaBilt in windows and doors. Those private brands carry structurally higher product margins and cannot be directly price-shopped on Amazon or at a competing hardware chain.

Equally important is the $1.83 billion 'Other Retail Services' line buried at the bottom of the Retail Home Improvement table. That bucket captures installed sales—where Lowe's coordinates vetted independent contractors to install kitchen cabinets, flooring, water heaters, and windows—alongside Lowe's Protection Plans, which generated $1.26 billion in long-term deferred revenue sitting on the balance sheet at FY2025 year-end. In Q3 FY2026, Home Services delivered its tenth consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales. Why does that matter to you as a long-term owner? Because Do-It-For-Me installation solves the exact friction point facing aging American homeowners who have home equity and aging houses, but neither the time nor the physical desire to tile a bathroom or wire a ceiling fan themselves.

Finally, keep a sharp eye on how FBM and ADG reshape Lowe's consolidated revenue mix over the next twenty-four months. In FY2025, FBM and ADG represented only 2.6% of total revenue because they were owned for just part of the year. By FY2026, that wholesale 'Other' segment is tracking near 7.5% to 8.5% of consolidated sales—roughly $7.5 billion to $8.0 billion annually. That revenue is stickier during DIY consumer pullbacks, yet it carries structurally lower gross margins than retail Home Décor and bears nearly $384 million a year in non-cash intangible amortization. Understanding this two-speed mix prevents you from panicking when consolidated gross margin ticks down 50 to 100 basis points—and forces you to track Retail Home Improvement segment margins separately in every quarterly 10-Q.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Never Blend Two Different Business Models Without Unpacking Them
callouts.text: When a high-margin retailer buys a wholesale building-materials distributor, consolidated margin percentages mechanically drop even if the core stores are thriving. Always separate Lowe's Retail Home Improvement segment (14.77% operating margin in Q2 FY2026) from its FBM/ADG wholesale segment (0.11% GAAP margin) before judging operational health.
